scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Origins are traced to the Udi Hills near Enugu, Nigeria.
The dance gained international prominence through 20th-century ethnographic research and competition, notably the 1952 Nigerian Festival of Arts and the 1970 post-Biafra War festival in Lagos.
on_screen: Map: Nigeria · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at festivals, coronations, marriage ceremonies, and harvest thanksgiving.
It serves as a display of youth vitality and cultural identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves a row of performers led by the 'Otu Ugo'.
Movement includes measured foot taps, waist shaking, arm swinging, and high-level acrobatics like flips and human towers.
The lead dancer sets the sequence, and the group follows with synchronized steps and stunts.
Watch for Human Tower.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (Hdl7myUxXSI)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Row formation led by the 'Otu Ugo', transitioning into human towers.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble typically includes the ogene (gong), ekwe (slit-drum), alo, gedegwu, ichaka (beaded gourd), and the oja (flute).
The flute player acts as the conductor, setting the pace for the dancers.
Listen for the ogene, ekwe, alo, gedegwu.
A high-energy, percussive sound dominated by the metallic ring of the ogene and the rhythmic, piercing melody of the oja flute, layered over the deep resonance of the ekwe slit-drum.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear short skirts or wrappers, often in bright colors like red, yellow, and green.
Seed rattles are worn at the waist and ankles to provide rhythmic accompaniment.
Leaders may wear tall plumes or carry a horsewhisk, while other dancers might carry palm-leaf fans.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Augustine Ene, a dancer who popularized the form in the 1950s, and the Nkpokiti dance group, which gained fame in 1970.
The Ile-Wonder Atilogwu of Umunede is a noted variant with specific techniques and sequences that have evolved over time.
Part of the broader Igbo dance tradition; some researchers have hypothesized links to other acrobatic traditions, though these remain unverified.
